utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to say hello to you all. It's case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this Monday, 3rd of July, 2006, I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom: The representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Scott; and all the Defence counsel present in the courtroom; the accused. I think one of them is absent today and has a reason for being so. I should also like to greet all and everyone here present. One of the Judges is absent today pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So we shall hear a witness today, but before bringing the witness in, I would like to render an oral decision in private session. Prior to that, I would like to state that last Friday the Trial Chamber rendered a decision pertaining to the oral motion filed by Prlic, who wished to be able to use a portable or laptop, or that the laptop be placed next to his Defence counsel. On a majority basis, the Trial Chamber did not grant the request. As far as I'm concerned, I filed a dissident opinion because I was in favour of the request that had been made. So may I invite you to read the decision as well as the dissenting opinion which has been handed over to you since Friday. In addition, I must render an oral decision in private session. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to inform the Chamber first of all that the Office of the Prosecutor is again acting in a way that makes it impossible for the Defence to properly prepare for its cross-examination of the witness. I say "again," because we discussed this prior to the arrival of the Spanish witness, BJ, and on that occasion Your Honours issued a ruling that cross-examination be separated from the examination-in-chief. My motion is that the Chamber should issue appropriate instructions to the Office of the Prosecutor to ensure a fair trial. The issue is the following: The Prosecutor has given the Defence erroneous information, and I believe the same information was given to the Chamber with respect to the extent and scope of the testimony to be expected. The initial information was disclosed through a summary. I will not repeat the name of today's witness because I don't know whether the witness is protected or not. This was in the viva voce chart, and the Prosecutor explicitly stated that the testimony referred only to the accused Slobodan Praljak. Two and a half weeks ago, however, the proofing chart was disclosed to the Defence, and this again does not contain all the elements Your Honours required in their ruling of the 30th of November, because in this proofing chart the paragraphs of the indictment are quoted, and they refer to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, to the issue of international armed conflict, and the qualifications in the indictment referring to all the accused. For example, in the proofing chart a reference is made to paragraphs 15, 16, 17, and 232 of the indictment, and then also to paragraphs referring explicitly with the name mentioned to the accused Prlic, Stojic, and Petkovic. I underline here that these are paragraphs 17.1, 17.2, and 17.3 of the indictment. Therefore, the viva voce chart gives one piece of information, and the proofing list provides a quite different piece of information, and these are contrary to each other. This puts the Defence in a position where it is hard for it to evaluate the main thrust of the witness testimony. This runs contrary to the Trial Chamber's decision of the 30th of November and clouds the issue not only for the Defence but also for the Chamber, which will find it more difficult to carry out its analysis of the evidence. Another argument we wish to put forward is that the Prosecutor is again disclosing the material too late. For example, on the 30th of June, on Friday, 12 new, untranslated documents were added, one of which is 400 pages long. Furthermore, the Prosecutor informed the Defence that no oral statement had been taken from that witness. This information was contained in a letter dated the 28th of June and handed to the Defence at the end of the sitting on that day. However, a synopsis was disclosed of the expected testimony. It is unclear how the synopsis or summary presented in the viva voce list in January this year could have been compiled if the witness was not interviewed. The summary is either therefore fabricated, which we don't believe to be the case, or it is based on some other material which should have been disclosed to the Defence. In any case, the Prosecutor explicitly states that there is no written statement taken from the witness. There may be notes taken by the Office of the Prosecutor during an interview with the witness; however, if these exist, we believe that this material should be disclosed according to the Rules of Evidence. In any case, the Defence has not been sufficiently notified of the topic of that witness's testimony, and we believe we have to draw the Chamber's attention to this because it hinders us in our preparations for the examination of this witness who is to testify very extensively. Therefore, in my view, this is detrimental to the provisions of paragraphs 20.1 and 21.4 of the Statute ensuring the right to a fair trial, and we move that the Office of the Prosecutor should be made to present its materials in a transparent manner, specifying to which of the accused each testimony refers. We believe that the material tendered along with these witnesses should all be translated and disclosed in a timely manner, and in view of the recess which has been planned, I move that the Chamber order the Prosecutor to present to the Defence a list of the witnesses to be called after the summer break, including a precise proofing chart for each witness. I move that this be done before the summer recess so that the Defence can properly prepare for the resumption of the trial. The Defence has been unable to prepare for the cross-examination of the current witness, so we move that once again, the cross-examination be separated from the examination-in-chief, or the witness be postponed. My colleagues are reminding me to add another point. We ask that the Office of the Prosecutor disclose the notes, if any, about its interview with the witness and to tell us explicitly on how many occasions they contacted and interviewed the witness. Thank you, Your Honours. If you have any questions as to details, I'll be happy to answer. I can only add that I sent two letters over the weekend to the Office of the Prosecutor concerning this issue, and we have received something else from the office of the Prosecutor. I haven't had a chance to look at it yet, but it is several excerpts from some newspaper articles. Once again, it's not a complete text but only excerpts and in an abbreviated form this seems to exist in the Croatian language, but I don't see it in English anywhere. So this is again some kind of incomplete material presented at the last minute, although I do have to concede it's not extensive, but it may be important. We now have to conduct a search through our own materials to see whether we have anything that is connected to it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Kovacic, just a short question I'd like to put to you before summing up what you've just said and before giving the floor to Mr. Scott. I read with a great deal of interest these two letters which you sent to Mr. Scott, and I realise that you mentioned having received the information on Friday and that you could not see your client before Monday morning. I want to make sure that on the Sunday -- on the Saturday and the Sunday you cannot go see your client who is in the Detention Unit? Is that what is being applied here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand it, we can contact our clients on Saturdays and Sundays only with explicit approval from the Trial Chamber. However, even if this is not correct, if on Friday afternoon after 5.00 p.m. we receive materials, there is in the Detention Unit no longer the person who arranges for these contacts, so we have to wait until Saturday morning, and of course we have to look at the materials before we contact our clients, and then if and when we do see the client, he needs a reasonable amount of time to look through the pile of materials we bring. So for all practical purposes, if something is received on Friday in the late afternoon, it's useless for Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It's important to mention this, because it's very much in line with the decision that the Trial Chamber took. In other words, it's important that you be able to meet your client during the week, because you are in the courtroom every day of the week. This is why I had felt that it was important for you to be able to go and see your clients on the Friday, and this is why there is no hearing on Fridays. Then, of course, if you receive the documents at 5.30 p.m., you have a difficult dilemma, and you can only see your client on Mondays. But as the hearing resumes on Monday afternoon, you can see your client on the Monday morning. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you are on your feet. I shall give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, in connection with what Mr. Kovacic has said. On Friday afternoon we received the list of 12 new documents which are not on the list presented in January of this year. The adding of documents without proper reason and an appropriate request is again happening, and then we have to conduct a search. At the start of these proceedings we had 9.490 documents. Now we have 9.673.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may add something to what I said about this event of Friday. My co-counsel and I saw our client on Friday morning and agreed on some questions to be put during this testimony and things to be put to the witness, and then in that afternoon we received these 12 documents, one of which is a 400-page book. Therefore, our visit of Friday morning was useless. The facts have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague has also prompted me to say that new documents have also arrived for a witness planned for next week. They are not translated and they are incomplete, but we have not yet discussed this with the Office of the Prosecutor. However, there is a possibility we will have a problem with the next witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to join my own request to those put forward by my colleagues and present a few additional arguments in connection with the exhibits or evidence we received on Friday, but may we go into private session before I do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're currently back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I can speak on behalf of all the accused. I arrived here in the hope that the trial would be fair, which also means expeditious. At a Pre-Trial Conference, Your Honour gave me the possibility of expressing my doubts as to the way of proceeding of the Prosecutor who is using a thousand fragments of a broken mirror to distort a picture and to distort the responsibility of individuals. I want to know when, where, and under what circumstances and in what manner, through an omission or through an action, whether by word or deed or thought, I did something wrong, because then I will be able to receive Your Honour's verdict with a tranquil mind. However, we are constantly brought into a position where the Prosecutor, whose case had to be complete on the day it was submitted in detail, keeps coming up with new things. And because this Tribunal also has its political dimension, for several years before I was indicted people were mentioning my name as a possible indictee. Years have gone by, and we are in detention contrary to human rights. Before this Tribunal the trial might last at least three or four years, and to this day we still don't have a clear list as to when, where, how, in what way. We are presented with witnesses who deal with all kinds of analyses; political, historical, sociological, psychological, and I have no idea where all this is heading. Thank you, Your Honours, for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. I shall pick up on what you've just said before giving the floor to Mr. Scott. Admittedly, when documents are introduced at the last minute this does affect the accused, and he starts wondering about it because he doesn't know what he is being charged with. Any new information does render the accused somewhat perplexed. And the Defence counsel have told us that there are 12 new documents that the Prosecution has since the month of January. Why is it that it has taken six months to disclose these documents? This is the first question. The second question: According to what I have understood, the witness in question has provided no written statement. There is no written statement. The Defence counsel and the Bench would like to know whether informal discussions have taken place with a view to bringing the witness here. Third question: On the face of document 9.673, a book, what looks like a book, 1989, 1975 -- 1989, 1999. This book is written in B/C/S. Unfortunately, I don't speak the language. This book is a 347-page long book which is being provided at the last minute and which has not been translated. So I have a string of questions. The Prosecution has realised that since the proofing session and the list and those items pertaining to Article 15 -- paragraph 15, 232, on joint criminal enterprise and common purpose. Mr. Scott, could you tell us what all this is about? This working method, it surprises me all the more because I had been particularly attentive, and I did spend many hours during the pre-trial phase to address these questions. I had asked you quite clearly to tell us how you intended to run this -- your case. Were you going to move from the facts to individual responsibility of each accused pursuant to Article 7(1) and 7(3), and I also asked you when you intended to talk about criminal -- common criminal enterprise, or were you to start off by addressing joint criminal enterprise before talking about individual responsibility? To be quite honest with you, I don't know how you intend to proceed. We have witnesses who are being called to testify. From what I understand, the upcoming witness is going to address the issue of the criminal enterprise, so it would be useful for us to have a common thread so that the Bench know where you're going. And as part of a fair trial, it is important that the Defence counsel be able to prepare their cross-examination when a witness is called to testify. But it's going in all directions and we have problems. When I say it's going in all directions, it's that when you come to realise at the last minute that there are new exhibits or new documents which have not been translated, what's to be done? Mr. Scott, could you tell us, please, why it is that we still have to contend with these problems at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Mr. President. One of the recurring problems in these is that when the Defence raise these matters, the Court is continually given an exaggerated position and also incomplete information. Number one, as to the summaries that have been provided, the Prosecution, since January, has provided summaries for its witnesses and has updated and supplemented those summaries as needed on a regular basis. As at least -- at least as long ago as the 27th of March, 2006, we made further disclosures concerning today's witness and provided an additional summary that goes on for three pages. At that time, we indicated -- I won't mention the name at the moment, but we mentioned -- this was as of the 27th of March, 2006, we anticipate that this witness may be an early witness in the Prosecution case in late April or the first part of May. So the Defence have absolutely no basis whatsoever to claim any surprise about this witness being called or to prepare. They've known about the witness specifically and the additional supplementation since the 27th of March, and they were told that in fact this witness might very well have been called some weeks and weeks ago. So if anything, they've had more time to prepare, not less. But that information apparently -- in all the complaints that you've just heard from the other side, that information wasn't provided to the Chamber. Secondly, in terms of the documents, Your Honour, I do regret that there was a small number of documents that had not previously gone out. This is them. There's 29 pages. This is what we're talking about. On some of these pages there is one paragraph. Some of these pages there's one paragraph. This is it. They've had that since Friday. I regret that it didn't go out sooner. It's a very small amount of material, extremely small amount of material. In terms of the book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that's 29 pages long, what number is that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm talking about all of them together are 29 pages. Every document that's in this bundle totals 29 pages, apart from the book. So what we're talking about, these complaints that have now taken the last 45 minutes are about 29 pages of material, some pages of which only have one short paragraph on them. That's the nature of the complaint. That's the material. As to the book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when I asked you the number, that's so I could take a look at those 29 pages myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so, Your Honour. 9639, 9640, 9641, 9642 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we can't find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, fine, but if I asked you the question it's because I couldn't find those documents to look through them. I don't have them in hard copy form.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then I don't know why you wouldn't have them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have almost half a square metre -- cube metre of documents before me but I don't seem to have those particular pages. Perhaps you could lend me your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My copy is marked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But I don't know, Your Honour. I was told -- my understand was that they had gone out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is going to lend me a copy, I see. And of course I'll give the copy back to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- Your Honour, I'm told that they were in your bundle -- they should be in the Court's bundle that starts with 8012, and some of the documents, partly because of the issues that were raised, some of the documents were withdrawn, so I think now the only documents that are in the bundle are 9645 and 9649. But you should have those, Your Honour, in the bundle that begins, on the top, Exhibit 8012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I'm going to give these back to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As to the book, Your Honour, in the -- in the communication -- in the communication that we delivered on Friday, we specifically indicated the pages of the book that would be referenced and I think again, altogether, I think those books -- I think those pages total something like 20 pages of the book. So we didn't simply hand over a 400-page book and say here it is. We specifically gave the page numbers that would be referenced in connection with the witness, and I have a receipt on that indicating -- so indicating. So that's the situation with the book. All of this material, by the way, all these -- all these ones -- the things that have been discussed since Friday and complained about since Friday are all open-source materials, as -- as all these prior interviews that have been discussed this afternoon. Now, counsel has indicated that there's all sorts of prior inconsistent interviews by this witness that go back to 1994. Your Honour, as far as I know, the Defence counsel have the same access to internet and other resources that the Prosecution does. Again, this witness has been disclosed specifically since the 27th of March, indicating that he might in fact be called by first part of late April or early May. There has been -- it is now July. I think ample time could be made to go and research prior open-source interviews given by this witness. This witness is not a surprise by any stretch of the imagination and there's been an abundant amount of time to prepare for this witness. As to the witness statement, Your Honour, there is no -- as we said in our letter - I will say again - there is no witness statement for this witness. As we said in our letter, indeed, the witness was met, various of the transcripts, the presidential transcripts were reviewed with him, but no statement was taken from this witness. To assist the Defence in their preparations, at my direction a summary was prepared by which to provide additional information to the Defence as to the nature of this witness's testimony. Beyond that, Your Honour, in terms of the more general points the Court has made, I regret that the Court feels that the case does not have as much structure perhaps as the Court would like. I can only give the Chamber -- and we persist in our approach that we have said since last November, and that is that the case would proceed after an overview primarily on a chronological basis. What we have endeavoured to do, and in my submission I will dare say I think we've done it quite well, is that in the beginning of the case to provide the Chamber with an overview of a wide spectrum of witnesses, including high-level political witnesses, some victim witnesses, some experts, some witnesses from various municipalities, some of which we did in anticipation of the site visit so that the Chamber would have, when you went out to these various locations, you might have heard at least from one witness as to a number of these locations. That was absolutely done methodically. It was not by -- it was not at random, it was done with a purpose, and again I submit that by the time we close the case before the summer recess, adjourn for the summer recess, the Chamber will indeed have been provided an excellent overview of the case in various aspects at various levels, but from the high political level, the overview such as today's witness down to a number of victim witnesses who have given the Court a taste, a sampling of the kind evidence these witnesses give. Once we complete the overview of the witnesses, we will then proceed, as I've indicated since last November, primarily in a chronological order through the events in the indictment. Now, sprinkled through there there will be other experts, there will be other political witnesses, but that will be the basic nature of the presentation, will be generally a chronological approach with some adjustments and some additions of additional types of witnesses, as I just mentioned. In our view, Your Honour, we're presenting the case in a way that makes sense and to assist the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before I give the floor to Mr. Karnavas, I'm going to summarise what you've already said. You have brought us an important element within the overall information, and you said that the witnesses presented so far had an essential purpose and that was to give the Trial Chamber an overview of a chronological basis for what happened. So I think that that's how we're going to have to understand the witnesses that have come into the courtroom to testify until next week, and after the recess we're going to start off by going in-depth with the other problems. Then you also told me that with respect to the 12 new documents, which in fact were only 29 pages in all, that there were a few documents that were very short, and I was able to note that myself, and other documents that one could get through very quickly. So I take note of that, and I see that you're right on that score. And you have not answered the question, that is to say how, as of August, you are going to schedule the witnesses and whether the Defence will have the names of those witnesses well on time, and the documents, of course, so that they can know and we can know how we stand and where we're going. Having said that, Mr. Karnavas was on his feet. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours again. I can understand the Prosecutor having some problems. It's early on in the case. But I think - let's be honest - if this witness was going to be called earlier, why is it that this late in the day we're getting this new material? The Prosecution says that it's only 28 pages. The original version, the B/C/S version, was not provided. With all due respect to translators, sometimes nuances are important, linguistic nuances, so we do need the original versions, plus it's the accused, most of whom don't read English, would obviously need to look at the B/C/S version so they could know exactly what is going on, because, after all, they are entitled to assist in their own defence. It should be noted that normally we get notice of this just as the Court has adjourned for the weekend, everybody has walked out, and it's then that we get a document so it's too late to react. It would be nice, if they're going to do that, to do that before we adjourn so at least, if we have any problems, we can voice them early on. With respect to the book, the book has 20 pages they're going to make reference to. The book is in B/C/S, or Croatian. Those pages have not been translated, so the question is how is it that the Prosecution -- as I understand it, Mr. Scott does not speak B/C/S -- how is it that those 20 pages were -- were identified, and how does he intend to use those 20 pages when in fact there is no translation? Also, as the Court may well know, if you take 20 pages out of context out of 500 pages or so of a book and they're out of context, it might be necessary for the Defence to have the rest of the book to look it over, to read it, and what have you. The Prosecution claims that this is an open-source material. I should remind the Prosecutor that this is not just merely an Anglo-Saxon process or just a two adversarial process, because the Trial Chamber, the Judges, are entitled and in fact do like to come to court prepared. They do read material in advance, and so surely we cannot expect the Trial Chamber to be surfing through the internet in order to look for open-source material. That open-source material should be made available. If the Prosecution knows, if they know they're going to use open-source material, why can they not tell us that months in advance? Unless the Prosecution is telling us that as of the last day or so they decided -- they made that decision, or came across that information, hence the reason why such late notice. Lastly, I just wish to point out this issue with the witness and no statement. Here I have three binders. This was my reading material for the weekend in addition to all the other stuff I had to do to prepare for this particular witness. These are presidential transcripts, Your Honour. Now, I find it hard to believe that one would sit there with a witness and go through all these presidential transcripts and not generate something substantial other than a summary. If they're going through the presidential transcripts and the gentleman was indeed present during many, if not -- not all, but most of these -- these particular meetings, I assume that the gentleman was making statements or was clarifying points, giving his points of view. I think that's all discoverable. It's not sufficient -- it is not sufficient to have a mere summary. I think that there's nothing -- nothing prevents the Prosecution, first of all, from tape recording it, or from having somebody to take actual live notes. But I do think that we do -- we are owed some more explanations. How many times did they meet with him? What was the length of time? Now, I know that I'm -- I'm in an international court and I'm supposed to take everybody at their bona fides, but guess what - when my client is looking at a life sentence, I'm entitled to doubt, and I doubt. I'd like to know how many hours did they meet with this particular witness and whether they have a tape recording, why did they choose not to record everything verbatim as they went transcript-by-transcript. But I think we need to know a little bit more about this. I think it's only fair. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Kovacic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I really don't wish to take up any more time, but I just have to bring up a few small points for the record and to avoid any misunderstanding. My colleague of the Prosecution said that, among other things, one of my objections were the fact that we hadn't received the proofing chart on time. That's not true. I said that we had indeed received the proofing chart on time, so I confirm that for the record. So proofing -- the proofing chart wasn't the problem. The problem was a different one. The problem was that before that, during the pre-trial brief, we received a summary and a viva voce overview of the witnesses where it was stated that that witness will testify about those facts. That testimony in this particular case is against your client. That is to say in this case Mr. Praljak. And then two or three paragraphs were mentioned with respect to the testimony. Then we received the proofing chart, as my colleague said, somewhere towards the end of March, that said something quite different. Because in listing the paragraphs, the proofing chart said this goes to such-and-such counts in the indictment against your client. Those paragraphs in the indictment. So this has brought us into a position where we don't know what we're being offered because we are -- have received two contradictory pieces of information from the OTP. So that is why I objected. Now, about the open-source material that we just heard about. We can agree, and I can say that I agree with what Mr. Karnavas has said. In my letter to the Prosecutor, I say very specifically that I agree that he is not duty-bound to disclose these open-source materials, but in this case he quite obviously is going to and is just giving us small excerpts of -- snippets of translation from the document. He is obviously planning to examine the witness on those portions from the book. So it's no longer relevant whether we're talking about open-source material but we have to be given the material on time so that we can read through it and so that we can, A, follow the examination-in-chief; and B, prepare a proper cross-examination. Of course, I don't have to tell you that in order to be able to do that I have to read through all 400 pages and not just those few excerpts that I have been provided with. So that is the correction that I wish to make. And if, as the Prosecutor said a moment ago, if he mentioned that a witness would be coming, then he hasn't come, why didn't he provide us with all those documents earlier on but had to wait until this particular Friday -- or last Friday? That is why I'm objecting. This is repetitive. It is tactics. It is not the circumstances that the Prosecution finds himself in. I know that full well, that when the witness came again for proofing before the testimony it is normal that in going through his previous statement that another subject crops up and they have to find another document or they find a previous statement made by the witness and then disclose it to us. But it's very strange, Your Honour, that this always happens on a Friday and always after 5.00 or 6.00 p.m. So I don't agree with my colleague Mr. Karnavas when he showed us three binders. There's a misunderstanding. We have seven or eight, my colleague and I. Perhaps they copied it in double page copies. I see, just one language, I've been told, just English. Whereas we have the B/C/S, the Croatian and English in seven or eight binders, and then on Friday we are given a ninth binder. Your Honours, that is physically impossible to tend with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber is going to give an oral ruling with respect to the problem that has just been raised and which is linked to a previous problem, and I'm going to read the ruling. When 19th of June, 2006, (redacted) (redacted)Mr. Kovacic asked the Chamber to provide with -- to disclose -- that the Prosecution should disclose to the Defence all documents which were presented during the testimony of the witness in one of the official languages of the Trial Chamber and in the language of the accused at least three weeks before the witness arrives; and secondly, that the examination-in-chief of the witness be restricted to subjects which are mentioned in the 65 ter Rule and disclosure there. And Mr. Kovacic indicated the fact that there were discrepancies, significant ones, between the summaries and the documents which were disclosed to him by the Prosecutor. After having consolidated the statements of the witness and the counts in the indictment for the accused, Mr. Kovacic and Ms. Alaburic expressed their concern over the vast amounts of material which were presented through the witness testimony, and these two counsel have proposed that the Prosecution should indicate in very precise terms and specific terms before a witness comes in what counts of the indictment the documents that it wishes to present are going to refer to. In the opinion of the Defence, this will enable us to avoid situations whereby certain documents which are not needed for this case be shown the witness. In response, the Prosecutor said that in general terms he was fulfilling his disclosure obligations and said that the Prosecutor had certain difficulties with the translations (redacted) documents, because the documents were originally in Spanish, and that's where the problem lay. Apart from that, Mr. Kovacic drew the attention of the Trial Chamber to -- in letters of the 30th of June and 1st of July to the following questions: Number one, Mr. Kovacic asked that today's witness testimony be postponed, or the cross-examination be postponed until a later date. As Mr. Kovacic claims, the Prosecutor failed to provide him with the necessary material on time and did so just last Friday when they disclosed about 400 pages of which a certain number of pages, or 12 documents, were not translated. And a moment ago, the Prosecutor explained to us that those 12 documents are just 29 pages long and that although the bulk material was 400 pages, which is in fact a book covering a certain period of time, that in fact all they would be using would be some 20-odd pages from that book. Apart from that, the Prosecutor indicated that he disclosed to the Defence the summaries and that he did so on time. They were updated summaries and that that was after the 27th of March, 2006. The Trial Chamber conferred a moment ago and assessed that the -- and is of the opinion that the next witness will be able to be examined-in-chief and also cross-examined. However, the Trial Chamber would like to add the following proviso: The Trial Chamber is very much concerned because of problems of this nature and which could lead to a lengthy trial and unnecessary delay, and as the Prosecutor said a moment ago, the -- or, rather, the Defence said, the accused have the right to an expeditious trial. The Trial Chamber wishes to note that in keeping with court practice, the practice of this Tribunal in case law, and in keeping with Article 21.4 of the Statute, the Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecutor must, in general terms, provide the Defence with all the documents that it intends to present in calling witnesses, not only in one of the official languages of this Tribunal but also in the language of the accused. That means that when the documents appear in court, they must appear in one of the working languages and in B/C/S as well. The Trial Chamber would like to remind those present of the following: Public documents, such as UN Security Council Resolutions, the UN Secretary-General reports, and similar material need not be translated into the language of the accused. The Trial Chamber would also like to note that it is in the interests of an expeditious trial and fair trial that brief documents should be translated because it is simpler to do so and the Defence can be provided with those documents. If they are shorter documents, they need not necessarily be translated into the language of the accused. Of course, all this on condition that we are dealing with documents of lesser importance in the sense of not being very lengthy documents. But the Trial Chamber would also like to mention that this can only be an exception to the rule and not the general rule in the proceedings. As far as the disclosure of those documents is concerned and the deadlines within which they must be disclosed, the Trial Chamber considers that in keeping with Article 21 of the International Tribunal's Statute, the Prosecutor is duty-bound to supply the Defence with these documents on time so that the Defence can prepare the cross-examination in the proper way. Therefore, the Trial Chamber considers that all the documents that have been translated must be disclosed to the Defence at least two weeks before the witness appears. Two weeks. Only in exceptional situations, and if we are dealing with shorter documents and documents of lesser importance, can that deadline be reduced. However, should a case of that kind occur, the Prosecutor will be duty-bound expressly to ask for permission and table a request to the Trial Chamber for that to be done. So the principle is that disclosure of material must take place two weeks before the start of testimony. And if there is any deviation from that rule and principle permission must be asked of the Trial Chamber or waiver granted. In addition to this, the Trial Chamber considers that the Prosecutor must, in the extent to which that is possible, limit the examination-in-chief of the witness to the questions contained in the summaries pursuant to Rule 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal. From this, it would emerge that the documents which were provided to the Defence and which were compiled on the basis of the indictment and the counts in the indictment must correspond to the summaries. The Trial Chamber accepts the possibility of allowing the Prosecutor to expand the scope of the examination-in-chief and to examine the witness on certain issues that are not in the summary. However, there must have been mention of these topics, something that cropped up during the proofing sessions of the witness. In such cases, with all the technical means available, they must inform the Defence thereof so that the Defence for their part could prepare in a proper manner for the cross-examination of those witnesses. If during a proofing session a point that has been mentioned does not figure in the proofing chart and that the Prosecution would like to address this particular issue, it is important that the Prosecution instantly, via e-mail, telephone, or fax, contact the Defence counsel to inform them about that. Lastly, the Trial Chamber bids the Prosecutor to disclose to the Defence counsel and to introduce at the hearing only those documents - and I stress the fact - only introduce those documents which are strictly relevant to the case. Pursuant to the Prosecutor's motion of the 15th of June, the Trial Chamber will shortly rule on this matter. It is important to specify which exhibit refers to which count in the indictment. The Trial Chamber would like to remind the Prosecutor that it must disclose by the 4th of September at the latest a chart which will meet this requirement. This should be disclosed to the Bench and to the Defence counsel. We have thus rendered our oral decision on this particular matter. Mr. Murphy, you would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we go into private session very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in open session, I turn to the Prosecutor. How much time will you need for your examination-in-chief of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We estimate approximately six hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said six hours. We have planned to finish on Thursday at a quarter to 2.00. Therefore, once the Prosecution will have spent six hours on its cross-examination [as interpreted], it will then be for the Defence team to work something out. It's for you to tell us then who will be taking the floor first and how much time each Defence counsel will have. You need to be well disciplined. We don't wish to find ourselves in the same situation we found ourselves last week where you were all getting up to ask for extra time. I'm eager to hear the ruling that will be made by the Appeals Chamber on the length of the cross-examination. I hope this will settle a number of issues. In the meantime, we have addressed this issue in a fairly flexible manner, so you will be able to cross-examine this witness up until Thursday, quarter to 2.00, once the Prosecution has finished with this witness. The Prosecution has said that it needed six hours. I don't wish to intervene here, but more often than not we waste a lot of time because we don't talk about what is essential. As part of an expeditious trial, I think it would be important if all and everyone addressed the core of the matter. We know that these are the items which, at the end of the day, will be included in the Bench's judgement. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With the best of will and with the hardest work on the part of the Defence counsel and myself, I fail to understand what the essential issues are. If a witness of this importance with whom I have been in politics since 1989, held the highest posts at the relevant period and comes to testify against me, and his offices and posts were far higher than mine, and he held far more responsibility at the time than I did, I have to bring a vast amount of documents to prove that what he's saying is not correct. Therefore, in order to challenge the testimony of this witness, it is impossible to establish that the response can take the same amount of time as the examination-in-chief. I will be very happy if the major issues were clarified and then they could be teased out, separated out, but sometimes you have to bring here a large amount of documents to prove that there is a discrepancy between what the witness is saying in response to the Prosecutor and what we see as the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to facilitate planning of time, I must say that none of the Defence teams has finalised its standpoint, but I can say with certainty that I will need at least a whole day because, on the basis of the summary, I can say objectively that I will certainly need at least a day, but it might take more. And I hear that some of the other Defence teams will need as much time, if not more. Your Honours, I ask that at the end we spend two or three minutes on this proofing charge [as interpreted]. Here it says that the witness will be testifying to joint criminal enterprise and international armed conflict. We will agree that this is the chapeau of the whole indictment and has to be clarified. Furthermore, this witness is speaking of the period from 1991 to 1994, the entire time period covered by the indictment, from the first to the last day. And I am grateful to my client for pointing out that throughout this time, until the Washington agreements in 1994, this witness held the highest posts in the Republic of Croatia, and according to the Prosecution, the representatives of that government were involved in the joint criminal enterprise. Therefore, this is a major witness for us. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By Your Honours' leave, and I'm saying this because my colleague Mr. Kovacic began saying something that I thought we would be discussing after the examination-in-chief. I wish to add that in any case, Mr. Stojic's Defence expects to get more than one-sixth, at least two or three times more for this witness for reasons of relevance and the counts in the indictment the witness's testimony refers to, and also for reasons well known to the Trial Chamber, which are that it is quite impossible to conduct the cross-examination within the given time frame. I wish to say this to avoid giving the impression that we are haggling over the time period we need. I wish the Chamber to know in advance that, as far as Mr. Stojic's Defence is concerned, we will be asking for more time than used by the Prosecutor. I think that we will not have any problems in being granted that time in view of the principles that the Chamber has adhered to so far, but we wish to avoid raising this issue at the last moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, I thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, a couple of things(redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: (redacted) It makes a witness very, very nervous and anxious to be sitting there in a room by himself for this long period with no communication of what's happening. I think we should try to avoid this situation. Number two, I invite the Chamber to give us further guidance, then, in terms of the cross-examination length of time, because the Chamber has said since the beginning of trial that it would be the same time as the Prosecution, generally speaking - generally speaking - with some exceptions for cause shown. But as we have said before, Your Honour, we have to have some basis to make plans, and if the Chamber is going to entertain at all the types of time that is being estimated by the Defence this afternoon, then for one thing, we need to tell the witnesses next not to come. And it will be too late by the end of the week. We have other people, they have their own private lives, they are entitled to make schedules, they're entitled to know, and if they can't come next week because this witness is going to stay over, then we need to know that as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm eagerly expecting, like you are, the decision that will be rendered by the Appeals Chamber. Let me remind you that I had indicated that in the indictment we had three major areas: A, what focused on the joint criminal enterprise; two, what focused on individual criminal responsibility of each accused; and C, those things that occurred in the various municipalities. I had indicated at the time that the Prosecution could have dedicated one-third of its time on joint criminal enterprise, one-third of its time on individual criminal responsibility, and one-third of its time on the facts, and in the course of time all of this has vanished. And as I mentioned a while ago, I would now like to go which way the Prosecution is going. The Prosecution has told us that in the first part of the trial, until the 13th of July, it will provide an overview on a chronological basis. After that, we will see how you intend to address all the other matters. To respond to Ms. Nozica, who said that a lot of time would be needed, something which I have just realised which I hadn't realised before: This witness is 86 years old. So please be reminded of this and remember, try to put yourself in the shoes of this man who has to undertake a cross-examination for many hours. In addition, it might well be the case that when general matters are raised, I have invited the Defence to convene and to designate one Defence counsel who would lead the cross-examination. The other Defence counsel could then share out between them the other issues to be addressed. It seems that you have not been able to come to some understanding, but this is just an avenue you could follow. A number of Chambers have decided, in light of the time spent by cross-examination, it only amounted to 60 per cent for the person asking the questions. So when you turn round to me and say you need three times more than the Prosecution, this is not at all in line with the case law of this Tribunal. But I hope that the Appeals Chamber will also provide its ruling on this matter very quickly so that we all know, including the Bench, where we stand. For the time being, as I mentioned a while ago, as far as this witness is concerned, we will make sure that the cross-examination is completed by the end of the week. If you feel that, pursuant to the ruling rendered by the Appeals Chamber a number of issues have not been addressed, you can still ask for the witness to be called back. Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. My colleague Mr. Murphy has pointed out a misinterpretation. I did not say -- at least, I did not mean to say that we needed three more times than the Prosecutor, but on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Stojic, we do need more than one-sixth; at least twice as much. I did not mean to say twice as long as the Prosecutor took. I wish to tell Your Honours that I think I am not a rude person, an impolite person, and I would certainly not maltreat an elderly gentleman through my cross-examination, but this witness, elderly as he is, was chosen by the Prosecutor, and the defence of my defendant, of my client, must certainly override all other considerations, and I believe that this witness must answer all relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Time has run out and the witness will probably not appear before the break, so I wish to raise an issue which only at first glance has -- seems to have nothing to do with what has been said so far. The Office of the Prosecutor, according to the Statute, has a mission to restore peace and so on in the region. However, the mission of the Chamber is only to judge fairly. I have been here for two months. I am of average education, and it is still not clear to me where this trial is leading. I would feel much better, and I don't know if this issue has been regulated in the Statute - you will allow that I am not a lawyer, and I have not consulted my counsel on this issue - but I would feel much better if the Prosecutor would make a solemn declaration, just as the witnesses do, that he will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. If this is not something that is contained in the Statute, I believe it would make the minds of the accused much easier. We would enter these proceedings with a lot of more bona fide feeling. This, for you, for all of you here in the courtroom, is just a job, business as usual, but we are talking about a day or two in detention more or less for my co-accused and myself. So it is in our interest to have the proceedings be as expeditious as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be very brief, Mr. Praljak, please. We're going to have the break soon. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: If he says, "No, I never said this," how, then, when everything is over, can he come with his clear Communist conscience - because he has turned his coat several times in his lifetime - how can he come here and say the things he's going to say? And as for relevancy, this witness should go home at once if this is not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it's a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to respond to that. I know the Chamber has allowed the accused to get up and make certain statements. This is improper. The accused has got up and insulted a witness and talked about his credibility. I agree counsel are entitled to cross-examination, but an accused or any other person in this courtroom is not allowed to stand up and insult a witness, and also to make arguments. That's completely inappropriate conduct from Mr. Praljak. That should not be allowed, with all respect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, just for the record, Mr. Praljak, will say anything [indiscernible]. The gentleman was a communist. He turned over, and then he kept turning over with every particular government. THE PROSECUTOR: This is again argument. Now we're arguing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is not argument; this is fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The Prosecution knows that he was a member of the Communist Party, and then he turned. So what is the problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's ten minutes to 4.00. We shall resume in 20-minutes' time, at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Let us move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tell Mr. Scott that we're going to certainly take a break at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting -- while we're waiting, the gentleman was, as Mr. Praljak noted, he was a member of the government for -- with the Tudjman administration for the period relevant to the indictment. The indictment, if you look at paragraph 15, 16, it makes references to a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that the witness be excused. I thought we were ready to take the witness. If we're going to have a legal argument --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I suggest --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. If we have any additional legal argument, that the witness be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's not a legal argument, Your Honour. It's my suggestion that he may be subject to a warning because, under the indictment, it would -- one could conclude that he would also be a member of the joint criminal enterprise and therefore, as a suspect, he should be warned that he has certain rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let me first ask you whether you can hear the proceedings in your own language and the translation of what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give me your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat my question: Could you please state your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Josip Manolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 22nd of March, 1920.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what your functions were in 1991, 1992, and 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I was a Member of Parliament in the Croatian parliament. Then I was elected to the Presidency of Croatia, the highest collective organ of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. Then in 1990 and 1991, I was the Prime Minister of the Socialist Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I held the office of head of the office of the president of the republic, until 1993 in March when I was elected the Speaker of the Chamber of Counties, or the Upper House of parliament.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sir, have you already testified before an International Tribunal or a national court on the events that took place in ex-Yugoslavia, or is this the first time you're testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I am testifying before the International Criminal Tribunal. I have testified before a Croatian court once in a war crimes case. This was against General Norac et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you testified in the trial against General Norac as a Prosecution witness or as a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Thank you. Would you now go ahead and read the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, sir. I'm just going to give you some information about the proceedings this week. As you know, you have been asked by the Prosecution to appear as a witness. You've just taken the solemn declaration, which means that you are now a witness for justice. You're going to answer questions that are going to be put to you by the Prosecution first, and they have told us that they will need approximately six hours for their examination-in-chief. After that, the Defence counsel, sitting to your left, representing the accused, one of which is absent today for medical reasons but will be here tomorrow, will be asking you questions within the framework of what we call in common law the cross-examination. And the Judges facing you - normally there are four Judges, today there are three - can ask you questions at any point in time during the proceedings. You will notice that the type of questions asked are different depending on who is asking them. The Prosecution will be asking questions which will require a response about developments and events. The Defence will ask leading questions, which usually mean that they want a yes or no answer. The Judges sitting in front of you have a different approach, and they're going to ask questions if they need any points clarified, points that you have already raised in your answers, or because they think that it is in the interests of justice for them to ask the questions. If you have any difficulty in answering the questions, please let us know. In the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal there are certain provisions which allow a witness to object to making -- to answering questions which might tend to incriminate the witness. So that is something that can happen, although we have never encountered it yet. In this case, the Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question, and testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness. I should also like to tell you, at the request of the Defence, that they note that there is a general incrimination in the indictment that is -- comes under the heading of joint criminal enterprise beginning with 1991. Now, since you held posts in 1991, it could happen that you fall into that category. So the witness -- the Defence would like us to draw your attention to that matter. If you don't understand a question, ask the person to restate it. If you have any other difficulties, please let the Bench know. I have taken note of the fact that you were born in 1920, so if you need any rest, please let us know and we will take a break, because I'm sure you already know that it's very tiring answering questions incessantly. So if you do feel you need a rest, we'll take a break. Please ask us and we'll take a break. The normal proceedings are that we make breaks every hour and a half, and we take 20-minute breaks. So the next break will be taken at half past 5.00, and we reconvene 20 minutes later, and then go on working until 7.00 p.m. Tomorrow morning we start work at 9.00 and go on to 12.30. At 12.30 we take an hour and a half lunch break, and then reconvene in the afternoon at 2.00 and go on working until quarter past 5.00. Wednesday will be the same thing, and on Thursday we're sitting from 9.00 until 1.45. So those are general pieces of information that I wanted to give you before the examination-in-chief goes ahead so that we can work in the best possible conditions. You will also be shown documents and asked to comment. Having said that, I give the floor to Mr. Scott for the next hour and a half, and as I've already said, we'll be taking our break at half past 5.00. And of course we're going to subtract the time from your six hours. Time starts running now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Manolic. Sir, I want to run through some of your background fairly quickly again. Some of it's already been indicated in your response to questions from the Judges but nonetheless I'll go through certain parts of it quickly again. Mr. Manolic, you were born in Croatia in 1920; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During World War II you were a soldier and participant in the anti-fascist movement, the forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, a participant in the anti-fascist movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After the war, from 1948 to 1960, you were the head of the Croatian Republic's division of the Ministry of Internal Affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following this, for a time, from 1960 to 1965, you were the head of the Secretariat of Interior Affairs in the city of Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In 1965, you became a member of the parliament, the Croatian Republic parliament, from which you were expelled following the suppression of the 1971 Croatian spring movement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You returned to politics in approximately 1989 as one of the founders of the Croatian Democratic Union political party, or as it has been referred to in this case already, the HDZ, and you were the first president of the Executive Committee of the HDZ at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were then elected to parliament on the HDZ ticket in 1990 and 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As you've indicated, you were then -- you were Prime Minister. You were the Prime Minister of Croatia in 1990 and 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: From August, 1990, to August, 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were a member of a body called the Presidential Defence and National Security Council in 1993? Is that correct? Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were then named the president of the Upper House, or Chamber, of parliament called the House of Counties, I understand, and you were in that position from approximately March, 1993, to March of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Until April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that one of your close political associates or colleagues from this time was a man named Stipe Mesic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And since his name will feature in some of the documents and testimony that we'll hear in the next day or two, during the period of time 1991, 1993, you've given us your positions. Can you briefly indicate, what was Mr. Mesic's position in the Croatian government? And I'm using that term broadly to include the legislative, the executive, any branch of the government. What were his positions in the government at the time you held the positions you've told us this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: I have known Mesic since 1965, in the Sabor parliament of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. He suffered in 1971 in the reformist movement, just like I did, when his mandate was taken away, just as it was from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what position -- if I can direct your attention particularly to 1991, 1992, what positions did Mr. Mesic hold in the Croatian government at that time, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: His position in 1990, he was first of all secretary of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, then he was the president of the Executive Council, and in 1990, when on the 30th of May the Croatian government was constituted, he was appointed Prime Minister of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So he was the Prime Minister, essentially, that preceded you in that position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Since he was supposed to go to Belgrade to become president of the federal top body, that is to say the Yugoslav state Presidency, I took over the post of Prime Minister of the Croatian government. So he was the Prime Minister of the Croatian government from only three months before he went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during the time period we're discussing now, did Mr. Mesic hold any office or position in the parliament, in the Croatian parliament or Sabor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: As a member of the Yugoslav state Presidency and later on president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, he could not have been a member of the parliament or Sabor in Croatia. He became Member of Parliament in the subsequent elections of 1992 when he was elected to the Croatian Sabor, parliament, and when he became president of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in going forward with your testimony, I would like to in some sense go to the end of the story and then we will come back and work forward again. Did there come a time in approximately 1994 that you and Mr. Mesic left the Tudjman government and left the HDZ political party?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we get into this line of questioning - excuse me, sir - I notice that we're only focusing on Mr. Mesic, who is currently the president. Now, I assume they're either going to bring Mr. Mesic here to testify, but I certainly would object to having this gentleman be speaking on behalf of Mr. Mesic. I think that's a whole different line of questioning. So he can speak about himself, but I would object to trying to somehow use this gentleman as an opportunity to talk about Mr. Mesic's state of mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I repeat the question, sir: Did there come a time in approximately 1994 that you and Mr. Mesic left the Tudjman government and left the HDZ political party?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's common knowledge. It was well known that we didn't agree with certain policies and therefore could no longer remain within the HDZ. I was excluded. They threw me out on the basis of articles in Feral Tribune, a magazine, and Globus, another journal that is accessible to the public. Now, as Mr. Mesic went to join another party that he established, he didn't -- he wasn't actually excluded and thrown out of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate date? It doesn't have to be the day, I don't believe, but perhaps the month, approximately, you left the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: I think I was expelled around the 20th of April, because on the 25th of April we had already established a new party, the Croatian Independent Democrats. So it was between the 10th and 20th of April that I was expelled from the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, a few moments ago you said that "It was well known that we didn't agree with certain policies and therefore could no longer remain within the HDZ." Could you tell the Judges what policies that you disagreed with.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: We did not agree, first and foremost, with respect to the policy being waged towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, we did not agree on policy matters with respect to the functioning of a State of Croatia based on the rule of law. That is to say there were not sufficient reactions to crimes that had been committed during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: And third, the third point of discord, was inter-party divergence, which isn't as essential because we objected to the authoritarian way in which the party was being led.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The authoritarian way in which the party was -- the HDZ party was being led?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the HDZ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was leading the party in an authoritarian way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: That means that he made decisions himself at will and that in a way he excluded the other members of the party. He left them aside, marginalised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say "he," sir, who are the individuals you are talking about now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about President Tudjman. That was the question as far as I understood it. You asked me what did I not agree with Mr. Tudjman -- President Tudjman with. First of all, his policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina; secondly, with respect to the functioning of Croatia based on the rule of law; and an auxiliary question which had to do with inter-party relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to your first reason that you've told us now, and that was the policy -- Tudjman's policy -- President Tudjman's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us how your view and Mr. Mesic's view differed from President Tudjman's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but before the witness answers that question, could we be precise as to the time period? I think the witness testified that his leaving of the party was in 1994, but it would be interesting to know the time period to which the policy of the party related to which he objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will come to that. If Mr. -- If the witness can first state the disagreement, I'll ask him about the time that this disagreement developed. If we can just proceed in a logical way, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the problem. We're not sure that it is logical, and it may well be irrelevant unless Mr. Scott first establishes the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, logics will have it that if there is agreement or disagreement, we must specify a date. So start off with a date and then proceed to explain the differences of opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, when was the -- the brief history of this disagreement; when it started, and how long it continued.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be a whole book. I would have to state when certain things began. We can start discussing from the time the leadership was constituted that took over power on the 30th of May, 1990. We were united then, pursuing a uniform policy. There were no differences between us. The differences emerged later on, and our relationships with Bosnia-Herzegovina and the then leadership were quite proper at the time. The president or, rather, Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Pelivan, and I was Prime Minister of the Croatian government, we had satisfactory cooperation at that period of time. And with the Bosnian Presidency and the Presidency of Croatia, those relations were very good and proper as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me -- let me stop you for one moment, please, just so the record is clear. You made a reference just now to Mr. Pelivan. He was the Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't look to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you -- so you started out, things were satisfactory, you've just told us, and can you tell -- in response to the President's question, when did you begin to notice or that it emerged or developed that there were in fact these differences or disagreements about the policy or conduct toward Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Those differences emerged with the first discussions between President Tudjman and Milosevic. On the 25th, I think it was, the 25th of March, 1991. That meeting was supposed to have been conducted between four people; Mr. Mesic from Croatia, and the vice-president at the time of the Federal Presidency of Yugoslavia -- what was his name? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: Jovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovic. Yes, that's right, Jovic. Very true. Mr. Jovic was supposed to attend the meeting. However, the agreement that was reached in the meantime when that meeting was scheduled to have it between four people, the agreement was between President Tudjman and Milosevic, that they should meet tete-a-tete, which meant that Jovic fell through and Mesic fell through. They no longer attended that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then these differences or disagreements continued on from approximately 1991 until you left in approximately April of 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP MANOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. With certain differences in the different periods. And I think somebody warned us of dates, and I think it is indeed very important to establish dates, to know -- to know when certain events took place so we can take a realistic view of those events, depending on when they occurred. Now, after that meeting that was held between Milosevic and President Tudjman, when the president returned, he did not make the agreement public at a broader forum. All he did was to inform me. I think he also informed President Mesic. Whether he informed anybody else about the contents of that meeting, I don't know. First of all, he said that they had agreed in principle about the issue of Bosnia-Herzegovina's division, in principle, but he didn't expound on that further. He was very pleased with that initial meeting he had with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir -- let me go back. We're going to come back to this in just a moment, but the question I put to you some minutes ago and then we started to talk about the time period. Before we go further into the detail, let me go back to the question I put to you earlier.
